title: Unusual case of Hashimoto’s encephalopathy and pseudo-obstruction in a patient with undiagnosed hypothyroidism: a case report
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old Indian man presented with a 2-day history of altered sensorium and abdominal distension. Over the preceding 3 months he had slow mentation, inattention, word‐finding difficulty, agitation, persecutory delusions, visual hallucinations, and constipation. He denied any medication use.

On examination he was drowsy with a hoarse voice, dry skin, puffy face, madarosis, cold extremities, and slowed reflexes. His abdomen was distended with absent bowel sounds. Chest and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed macrocytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 100 fL), leukopenia (3,900/mm3), and normal glucose, liver and kidney function, arterial blood gases, and electrolytes. Septic workup was sterile. Chest radiograph and ECG were normal. Abdominal ultrasound and plain radiographs demonstrated diffuse gaseous distension with dilated loops and air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed dilated small-bowel loops; whole‐body CT was otherwise unremarkable.

Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), ANA, and HIV serologies were normal. Thyroid examination was non-tender and without goiter. Neck CT showed a diffusely atrophic thyroid with low attenuation. Thyroid studies revealed TSH 76.5 µIU/mL (normal 0.39–3.55), FT4 0.1 ng/dL (0.75–1.54), and FT3 0.42 pg/mL (2.0–4.9). Serum anti-TPO antibodies were 581 U/mL (normal <60).

Brain MRI showed mild diffuse atrophy with prominent sulci, periventricular ooze on FLAIR, and T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in periventricular and subcortical white matter. EEG was normal. CSF examination revealed elevated protein, normal glucose, and was positive for anti-TPO antibodies. Gut manometry demonstrated features of intestinal dysmotility.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious or inflammatory encephalopathy and gut obstruction were considered — “Our patient presented with encephalopathy with gut obstruction that could have indicated infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, toxic and metabolic aetiologies.”  
2. Chronic lead toxicity was excluded despite occupational exposure — “ruled out all possibility of close differential diagnoses such as chronic lead toxicity as he had occupational exposure to lead…”  
3. Megaloblastic anemia was excluded by normal B12 levels and blood counts — “…megaloblastic anaemia…”  
4. Gut neoplasia with sepsis was excluded by sterile septic profile and lack of mass on imaging — “…gut neoplasia with overwhelming sepsis…”  
5. Brain metastasis was excluded by unremarkable whole-body CT and absence of focal lesions on MRI — “…and brain metastasis.”  
6. Hashimoto’s encephalopathy was supported by high anti-TPO titers in serum and CSF and steroid responsiveness — “Our patient’s elevated anti-TPO antibodies in his serum and CSF and his response to steroid therapy seemed appropriate to establish a certain diagnosis.”  
7. Intestinal pseudo-obstruction due to hypothyroidism was supported by gut manometry and gradual improvement with thyroid hormone replacement — “Profound hypothyroidism can cause intestinal dysmotility, results in paralytic ileus and intestinal pseudo-obstruction. These features respond to the thyroid hormone replacement therapy gradually over time.”
